# Final technical summary: Residual Screening for Indoor Robot Localization

**Principal investigator:** Tessa Maren Halwick, Alderquay University  
**Award:** AQU-FIF-24-018, university Faculty Inquiry Fund; $78,000  
**Project period:** 1 January 2024–31 December 2025  
**Report accepted:** 20 February 2026  
**Archive and status check:** 30 September 2026

## Purpose and completed work

The project tested whether a residual-based observation screen improved indoor localization when recorded sensor streams contained specified corruptions. The research question concerned estimator behavior under a reproducible fault model. Completed outputs comprise a paired replay evaluation, a journal article, an institutional technical report, and a documented archive of recordings and analysis scripts.

The system combines a conventional localization filter with a screening rule that compares each incoming observation against its predicted residual distribution. Observations that cross the fixed screening threshold receive reduced weight. The screen uses information available to the estimator; the independent reference position is reserved for scoring. Both the baseline and screened estimator use the same motion model, initialization, and recorded input stream.

The university accepted the final report after an independent internal rerun of the primary analysis. The award is closed. Archive maintenance continued during 2026 through the faculty laboratory's existing university resources.

## Collection and evaluation design

Six differential-drive bench robots were used to record indoor trajectories during 2025. The archive contains 72 source trajectories: 12 development trajectories and 60 held-out evaluation trajectories. Each robot contributed two development trajectories and ten evaluation trajectories. Development trajectories were used to select the screening threshold and settle analysis code. They were excluded from the reported evaluation results.

The 60 evaluation trajectories were recorded in the same instrumented laboratory, with different path shapes and stopping patterns. Each robot operated alone. An independent optical reference system supplied positions for scoring. Reference positions were excluded from the estimator inputs. The reference-system calibration record was checked before collection; scoring nevertheless inherits the reference system's measurement uncertainty.

There were three mutually exclusive replay conditions, each assigned to 20 evaluation trajectories: contiguous observation dropout, persistent additive position bias, and delayed observations delivered with their original timestamps. A trajectory received one fixed condition. The faults were scripted in advance. Condition assignments, affected channels, and fault intervals were frozen before the evaluation runs.

For each evaluation trajectory, the baseline and screened estimator processed the same corrupted stream. The trajectory was the unit of analysis. Repeated software execution checked reproducibility without increasing the sample size. The six robots were repeated-use experimental assets of the same bench configuration; robot identity was retained in the analysis manifest.

## Outcome definition and results

For each estimator, horizontal position error was calculated at the scored timestamps against the optical reference. The median error within each trajectory was then calculated. The primary summary was the median of those 60 trajectory-level medians. Each trajectory therefore contributed one error summary, regardless of its number of scored timestamps.

The baseline primary summary was 0.50 m. The screened estimator's primary summary was 0.34 m. The difference between these two medians was 0.16 m, equivalent to a 32% reduction relative to the baseline summary.

The bootstrap 95% confidence interval for the reduction was 0.09 to 0.23 m. The analysis used 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples. Each resample retained the baseline and screened outputs together and sampled trajectories within robot, preserving each robot's contribution. The interval describes variation among trajectories conditional on the tested robots, room, fault assignments, and analysis procedure.

The pooled estimate was the prespecified primary result. The experiment was not powered to rank the three fault conditions or establish a benefit separately in every condition. Inspection of individual traces showed that screening sometimes discarded valid measurements after sharp turns. Those trace inspections were diagnostic observations, without a prespecified event-counting protocol or an estimated population frequency.

## Reproducibility and released materials

The *Halwick Indoor Replay Collection*, version 1.0, was deposited in Alderquay University's institutional repository on 28 February 2026. It contains the 72 source trajectories, reference-position streams, development/evaluation assignments, evaluation fault manifests, and documentation of coordinate frames and timestamps. Faulted streams are generated from the source recordings by the supplied replay scripts.

The repository also contains the estimator configurations, frozen screening threshold, analysis script, and bootstrap seed. Data are released under CC BY 4.0 and project code under the MIT License. The release contains laboratory robot and sensor records. Student assessment records are maintained separately under the teaching study's access controls.

A second group member, Ravi Nolan Keswick, independently reproduced the primary summaries from the frozen archive before report acceptance. The reproduction used the archived configurations and bootstrap seed. Its purpose was to check executable provenance and the reported summaries; it used the original recordings.

## Interpretation and limitations

The study was a single-robot, offline replay evaluation in one room. Results are conditional on the six robots used for collection. Because observations were replayed, the estimator's output could not change the robot's subsequent motion. Feedback between estimation failure and control action was absent from the experiment.

Fault selection was fixed before execution. The evaluation consequently provides limited evidence about an adversary that observes the screen and adapts its behavior. The observation and motion models were shared between the two estimators, so model misspecification common to both methods remains an additional limitation.

The December 2025 article and this report use the same evaluation dataset; the August 2026 calibration article is a subsequent analysis of that material.

## 1. Sensor corruption and residual screening

**Halwick, T. M.; Westrall, L. C. (2021). “Residual screening under structured sensor corruption.” Journal of Sensor Integrity and Estimation.**  
DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-sensor-security-career-pi.2021.1

Published in November 2021. This article reports dissertation experiments on residual screening when the assumed observation model is violated. The evidence consists of simulation and recorded sensor-stream analyses. It distinguishes isolated outliers from sustained corruption and documents circumstances in which screening removes useful information.

Halwick designed the corruption experiments, implemented the analysis, and wrote the initial manuscript. Westrall supervised the dissertation and contributed to interpretation. The article's empirical comparisons use fixed corruption processes and describe performance conditional on those processes.

## 2. Experimental comparison of replayed faults

**Halwick, T. M.; Westrall, L. C. (2023). “Paired replay designs for comparing localization filters under observation faults.” Transactions on Experimental Robot Security.**  
DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-sensor-security-career-pi.2023.1

Published in June 2023 during Halwick's postdoctoral appointment. The article develops an experimental workflow in which competing estimators receive identical corrupted recordings. Its contribution is control of comparison conditions and explicit identification of the experimental unit. It explains the distinction between repeated deterministic execution and independent observations.

Halwick implemented the replay workflow and performed the comparisons; Westrall contributed the study design and methodological critique. The article uses material collected during the Dunmere Crest appointment, preceding the Alderquay evaluation archive.

## 3. Completed indoor-robot evaluation

**Halwick, T. M. (2025). “Trajectory-level evaluation of residual screening for indoor robot localization.” Journal of Reproducible Autonomous Systems Experiments.**  
DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-sensor-security-career-pi.2025.1

Published in December 2025. This sole-authored article reports the held-out replay evaluation summarized in the final project report. Its primary outcome is the median of trajectory-level median horizontal errors. The article and final report describe the same evaluation. The February 2026 repository deposit supplies the frozen data and scripts supporting the published analysis.

Halwick performed the study design, estimator development, analysis, and writing. Funding: Alderquay University Faculty Inquiry Fund, AQU-FIF-24-018. The methods section documents trajectory pairing, threshold selection on development recordings, and bootstrap resampling within robot.

# Sensor Systems Laboratory: teaching and assessment record

**Instructor:** Tessa Maren Halwick, Alderquay University  
**Record updated:** 30 September 2026

## Course context and instruction

The undergraduate Sensor Systems Laboratory connects measurement, estimation, and security through small experiments with recorded and live sensor observations. Halwick taught the completed fall 2024 and fall 2025 offerings. Enrollment was 24 students in 2024 and 28 students in 2025, for 52 students across the two offerings. Students worked in rotating laboratory groups because research and teaching shared the six bench robots. The assessment unit was the individual student.

The fall 2026 offering began on 24 August 2026 with 26 enrolled students. Entry assessments have been administered. Consent decisions remain sealed until grades are final. Assessment collection follows the same course protocol covered by AQU-ED-2024-017; research analysis of the current cohort has not begun. The completed-cohort results below include only the 2024 and 2025 offerings.

The course has three stated learning objectives: identify assumptions in an observation model; construct a comparison that isolates an estimator change from a data change; and interpret an uncertainty interval without turning it into a claim of universal reliability. Students encounter these objectives in exercises, written explanations, and the assessment rubric.

Early exercises ask students to examine clean recordings and explain how sensor measurements differ from reference position. Later exercises introduce dropout and biased readings. Students compare two estimators on the same recording and account for differences in initialization or preprocessing. They identify the trajectory as the independent comparison unit and explain how treating every timestamp as an independent replicate affects estimated uncertainty.

## Relationship to research practice

The course uses the group's replay framework and simplified examples derived from its research workflow. Teaching recordings are kept separate from the held-out research evaluation set. The research screening threshold was selected using the project's development recordings.

Students produce a manifest recording the input recording, injected fault, estimator configuration, and output files. A second group attempts to rerun the comparison from that manifest. The submitted work includes the original analysis, the reproduction record, and a short explanation of any discrepancy. The instructor assesses whether the comparison can be reconstructed and whether the reported conclusion follows from the documented analysis.

Discussions of screened observations emphasize that rejecting a measurement may reduce one error summary while worsening another trajectory or excluding valid information. Students explain this limitation alongside their plotted results. Instruction covers empirical comparisons and statistical uncertainty.

## Learning assessment

An institutional determination dated 12 August 2024, reference AQU-ED-2024-017, classified the specified analysis of normal educational assessments as exempt educational research. Its scope includes repeated offerings of this course using the specified assessment and consent procedures. It does not authorize unrelated human-participant studies. Participation in research analysis is voluntary, and consent decisions are withheld from the instructor until course grades are finalized.

Of the 52 enrolled students in the completed offerings, 44 consented to use of their assessments: 20 from the 2024 offering and 24 from the 2025 offering. All 44 consenting students had paired entry and exit assessments. The other eight students completed ordinary course activities but were excluded from the research analysis.

The assessment used parallel forms scored with a 12-point rubric covering model assumptions, comparison design, and uncertainty interpretation. Deidentified responses were shuffled before scoring so the scorer did not see student names or whether a response was from entry or exit. The mean paired gain was 2.1 points, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 1.4 to 2.8 points. Resampling used paired student records within course offering.

This is a descriptive result from consenting students in two classes. There was no randomized comparison group. Other instruction, practice effects, and maturation remain possible explanations for part of the observed change. Selective consent remains uncontrolled, and scoring judgment adds uncertainty beyond the bootstrap interval. No retention assessment or external transfer task was administered.

## Access and public engagement

Recorded-data versions of the exercises were available to students who could not attend an equipment session. Instructions included text descriptions of plots and required numerical summaries alongside color-coded graphics. These provisions are documented course practices; their effects were not separately estimated.

The department held a public robot demonstration in April 2025. Visitors watched a robot follow an indoor route and viewed its estimated position. The event record consists of the route script and display materials.

# Final technical summary: Residual Screening for Indoor Robot Localization

**Principal investigator:** Tessa Maren Halwick, Alderquay University  
**Award:** AQU-FIF-24-018, university Faculty Inquiry Fund; $78,000  
**Project period:** 1 January 2024–31 December 2025  
**Report accepted:** 20 February 2026  
**Archive and status check:** 30 September 2026

## Purpose and completed work

The project tested whether a residual-based observation screen improved indoor localization when recorded sensor streams contained specified corruptions. The research question concerned estimator behavior under a reproducible fault model. Completed outputs comprise a paired replay evaluation, a journal article, an institutional technical report, and a documented archive of recordings and analysis scripts.

The system combines a conventional localization filter with a screening rule that compares each incoming observation against its predicted residual distribution. Observations that cross the fixed screening threshold receive reduced weight. The screen uses information available to the estimator; the independent reference position is reserved for scoring. Both the baseline and screened estimator use the same motion model, initialization, and recorded input stream.

The university accepted the final report after an independent internal rerun of the primary analysis. The award is closed. Archive maintenance continued during 2026 through the faculty laboratory's existing university resources.

## Collection and evaluation design

Six differential-drive bench robots were used to record indoor trajectories during 2025. The archive contains 72 source trajectories: 12 development trajectories and 60 held-out evaluation trajectories. Each robot contributed two development trajectories and ten evaluation trajectories. Development trajectories were used to select the screening threshold and settle analysis code. They were excluded from the reported evaluation results.

The 60 evaluation trajectories were recorded in the same instrumented laboratory, with different path shapes and stopping patterns. Each robot operated alone. An independent optical reference system supplied positions for scoring. Reference positions were excluded from the estimator inputs. The reference-system calibration record was checked before collection; scoring nevertheless inherits the reference system's measurement uncertainty.

There were three mutually exclusive replay conditions, each assigned to 20 evaluation trajectories: contiguous observation dropout, persistent additive position bias, and delayed observations delivered with their original timestamps. A trajectory received one fixed condition. The faults were scripted in advance. Condition assignments, affected channels, and fault intervals were frozen before the evaluation runs.

For each evaluation trajectory, the baseline and screened estimator processed the same corrupted stream. The trajectory was the unit of analysis. Repeated software execution checked reproducibility without increasing the sample size. The six robots were repeated-use experimental assets of the same bench configuration; robot identity was retained in the analysis manifest.

## Outcome definition and results

For each estimator, horizontal position error was calculated at the scored timestamps against the optical reference. The median error within each trajectory was then calculated. The primary summary was the median of those 60 trajectory-level medians. Each trajectory therefore contributed one error summary, regardless of its number of scored timestamps.

The baseline primary summary was 0.50 m. The screened estimator's primary summary was 0.34 m. The difference between these two medians was 0.16 m, equivalent to a 32% reduction relative to the baseline summary.

The bootstrap 95% confidence interval for the reduction was 0.09 to 0.23 m. The analysis used 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples. Each resample retained the baseline and screened outputs together and sampled trajectories within robot, preserving each robot's contribution. The interval describes variation among trajectories conditional on the tested robots, room, fault assignments, and analysis procedure.

The pooled estimate was the prespecified primary result. The experiment was not powered to rank the three fault conditions or establish a benefit separately in every condition. Inspection of individual traces showed that screening sometimes discarded valid measurements after sharp turns. Those trace inspections were diagnostic observations, without a prespecified event-counting protocol or an estimated population frequency.

## Reproducibility and released materials

The *Halwick Indoor Replay Collection*, version 1.0, was deposited in Alderquay University's institutional repository on 28 February 2026. It contains the 72 source trajectories, reference-position streams, development/evaluation assignments, evaluation fault manifests, and documentation of coordinate frames and timestamps. Faulted streams are generated from the source recordings by the supplied replay scripts.

The repository also contains the estimator configurations, frozen screening threshold, analysis script, and bootstrap seed. Data are released under CC BY 4.0 and project code under the MIT License. The release contains laboratory robot and sensor records. Student assessment records are maintained separately under the teaching study's access controls.

A second group member, Ravi Nolan Keswick, independently reproduced the primary summaries from the frozen archive before report acceptance. The reproduction used the archived configurations and bootstrap seed. Its purpose was to check executable provenance and the reported summaries; it used the original recordings.

## Interpretation and limitations

Results are conditional on the six robots and one room. The study did not test closed-loop control or multiple robots. Because observations were replayed, the estimator's output could not change the robot's subsequent motion. Feedback between estimation failure and control action was absent from the experiment.

Fault selection was fixed before execution. The evaluation consequently provides limited evidence about an adversary that observes the screen and adapts its behavior. The observation and motion models were shared between the two estimators, so model misspecification common to both methods remains an additional limitation.

Collection and testing were confined to the indoor laboratory; public-road deployments: 0. The study's measurements concern localization error. Collision risk, coordinated agent failures, and communication-dependent behavior were outside the measured outcomes. The December 2025 article and this report use the same evaluation dataset; the August 2026 calibration article is a subsequent analysis of that material.

The undergraduate Sensor Systems Laboratory connects measurement, estimation, and security through small experiments with recorded and live sensor observations. The course has three stated learning objectives: identify assumptions in an observation model; construct a comparison that isolates an estimator change from a data change; and interpret an uncertainty interval without turning it into a claim of universal reliability. Students encounter these objectives in exercises, written explanations, and the assessment rubric.

Early exercises ask students to examine clean recordings and explain how sensor measurements differ from reference position. Later exercises introduce dropout and biased readings. Students compare two estimators on the same recording and account for differences in initialization or preprocessing. They identify the trajectory as the independent comparison unit and explain how treating every timestamp as an independent replicate affects estimated uncertainty.

## Relationship to research practice

The course uses the group's replay framework and simplified examples derived from its research workflow. Teaching recordings are kept separate from the held-out research evaluation set. The research screening threshold was selected using the project's development recordings.

Students produce a manifest recording the input recording, injected fault, estimator configuration, and output files. A second group attempts to rerun the comparison from that manifest. The submitted work includes the original analysis, the reproduction record, and a short explanation of any discrepancy. The instructor assesses whether the comparison can be reconstructed and whether the reported conclusion follows from the documented analysis.

Discussions of screened observations emphasize that rejecting a measurement may reduce one error summary while worsening another trajectory or excluding valid information. Students explain this limitation alongside their plotted results. Instruction covers empirical comparisons and statistical uncertainty; formal verification is outside the current syllabus.
